title: Earth Hero: designing the gamification layer
tagline: Tech Fleet · Client UX research & product design
summary: Volunteer client work through Tech Fleet Community DAO for Earth Hero, a climate-action app. With a design partner on a cross-functional team, I designed a gamification layer — quests, Earth Points, team challenges and a growing avatar — and wrote the usability study to find out whether players read it the way it was intended.
highlights: A component library and named colour system built for the layer, not bolted onto it
A moderated remote usability study written around one question: are people experiencing the gamification the way we meant?
Recommendations presented to the client, who took elements into the live product

hero.title: Earth Hero: designing the gamification layer
hero.subtitle: Turning climate action into something a person would come back to, and then testing whether it read the way we intended.
hero.summary: Earth Hero is a climate-action app. Through Tech Fleet Community DAO — a volunteer collective that runs real client engagements — I worked with a design partner on a cross-functional team to design the layer that makes daily action feel like progress: quests, Earth Points, team challenges, and an avatar that grows as you use it.

overview.title: Climate action is a habit problem before it is an information problem
overview.description: People who already care about their footprint still stop logging actions after a week. The app did not need to convince anyone that climate change matters; it needed to make returning tomorrow feel worth it. That is a motivation design problem, and the risk with motivation design is that it is easy to build something that looks engaging and is read by users as noise, or worse, as pressure.

challenge.title: Sketch it on paper before it can hide behind a component
challenge.description: The work started on paper and whiteboards — flows, screen skeletons, and a wheel mapping the five impact pillars the app organises itself around. Working rough for as long as possible kept the argument about whether the mechanic made sense, rather than about whether the button was the right blue.

media.alt: Two hand-drawn paper wireframes: screen skeletons, a progress bar sketch and annotations in pen
media.title: Paper wireframes from the first pass

solution.title: One growing avatar, five pillars, and a vocabulary that holds together
solution.description: The layer is built from a small set of pieces that repeat. An avatar moves through five named stages so progress is visible without a number. Five pillar icons tag every action, so a person can see what kind of impact they are having rather than only how much. Colour is organised by element — Earth, Water and Air — each with dark, base and light steps, so a screen can be tinted by meaning instead of decoration.

steps.description: The entry point: pick something to do rather than read about what you could do.

steps.title: Log a daily action
steps.description: The smallest repeatable unit, tagged to one of the five pillars.

steps.title: Earn Earth Points
steps.description: Progress shown on a bar tied to the avatar's growth stage, not an abstract score.

steps.title: Join a team
steps.description: Individual action rolls up into a team's Weekly Challenge.

steps.title: See where you stand
steps.description: A leaderboard and a team progress view close the loop.

modules.title: Avatar stages
modules.description: Seed → Sprouted → Developed roots → Vegetative → Budding. Growth carries the progress, so the screen does not have to lead with a score.

modules.title: Five impact pillars
modules.description: Emissions, social, political, biodiversity, and waste and consumption. Every action is tagged to one, which is what lets the app answer "what kind of difference did I make?"

modules.title: One component library
modules.description: Avatar states, progress-bar variants, pillar icons, community badges, buttons, vouchers and task cards, built once and reused across every screen.

impact.title: Written to find out if it was read the way we meant
impact.description: I wrote the usability study around a single question: are users experiencing the gamification elements in the intended way, and what impact do those elements have on them? Participants created a quest, chose a team, learned about Earth Points, logged a daily action, found their place on the Weekly Challenge leaderboard, and viewed their team's progress — with engagement, understanding, satisfaction and ease of use measured alongside. The study ran moderated and remote over Zoom and Google Meet: a short briefing, a series of questions, then a wrap-up.

friction.title: The revision list is the honest record
friction.description: The design moved through a long, colour-coded list of changes held as Done and Doing — progress-bar points that had to match the actual distribution of available points, consistency in the bottom navigation across every screen, a notification that fades rather than sits, recurring-action handling, and avatars grouped so a leaderboard could use them. Most of it is unglamorous. It is also where the layer stopped being a concept and became something that behaves consistently.

conclusion.title: What this shows, and what it does not
conclusion.description: Recommendations went to the client, and Earth Hero took elements of the work into its live product. What is shown here is the design system, the prototype, and the study as it was written and run — not the findings, which belong to the client engagement rather than to me. If you want to talk about what the sessions surfaced and how the recommendations were framed, that is a conversation I am glad to have.
